title: Build Your First Resume
subtitle: Zero experience? No problem.
videoTitle: How to Write a Resume With No Work Experience
description: Create a standout resume even with no work experience. Learn exactly what employers look for and how to make your skills shine.
keyPoints: Your resume is a marketing document — sell yourself!
No job experience? Use school projects, clubs, and volunteer work
Keep it to 1 page and use clean, readable formatting
Tailor your resume for each job you apply to
Proofread everything — typos are instant rejections

sections.title: What Goes on a Resume?
sections.content: Even with zero work experience, you have more to show than you think. A strong resume includes: your contact info, a brief objective statement, your education, any skills you have (even if learned in class), activities like clubs or sports, volunteer or community work, and any projects you're proud of. Think of each section as a story about who you are.

sections.title: The Skills Section is Your Secret Weapon
sections.content: Skills are divided into hard skills (specific, teachable abilities like 'Microsoft Excel' or 'Spanish') and soft skills (personality traits like 'teamwork' or 'communication'). List both! Even things you learned in school count — if you've used Google Slides, that's a digital skill. If you've worked on a group project, that's collaboration.

sections.title: Action Verbs Make You Sound Powerful
sections.content: Start every bullet point with a strong action verb. Instead of 'I helped with the bake sale,' write 'Organized and promoted a school fundraiser that raised $400.' The difference is massive. Use words like: led, created, managed, designed, assisted, trained, built, improved, solved, achieved.

title: Ace Your First Interview
subtitle: Turn nerves into confidence.
videoTitle: How to Answer Interview Questions — STAR Method
description: Master common interview questions, body language, and how to make a great first impression that gets you the job.
keyPoints: Research the company before you walk in the door
Use the STAR method: Situation, Task, Action, Result
Make eye contact and sit up straight — posture matters
Prepare 2–3 questions to ask the interviewer
Always send a thank-you message within 24 hours

sections.title: The STAR Method Explained
sections.content: STAR stands for Situation, Task, Action, Result. It's the secret formula for answering behavioral interview questions like 'Tell me about a time you solved a problem.' Start with the Situation (context), explain your Task (what you needed to do), describe your Action (what you actually did), and finish with the Result (what happened). Employers love concrete stories.

sections.title: Body Language is Half the Interview
sections.content: Before you say a word, your body is already communicating. Firm handshake, eye contact, and a genuine smile signal confidence. Sit up straight and lean forward slightly to show engagement. Avoid crossing your arms (defensive), looking at the floor (nervous), or fidgeting (anxious). Practice in a mirror — it really helps!

sections.title: Questions They WILL Ask You
sections.content: Every interviewer has a standard list. 'Tell me about yourself' (keep it to 60 seconds, focus on relevant skills and goals). 'Why do you want this job?' (show you researched them). 'What's your biggest weakness?' (pick something real, then explain how you're improving). 'Where do you see yourself in 5 years?' (show ambition but stay realistic).

game.title: 🎮 Hot Seat — Interview Simulator
game.instructions: Pick the BEST answer for each interview question. Wrong answers dock XP, right answers earn it. Can you pass the interview?

questions.question: The interviewer asks: 'Tell me about yourself.' What do you say?

answers.text: I'm 17, I live in Brooklyn, and I like gaming.
answers.feedback: Too personal and unfocused. Keep it professional!

answers.text: I'm a motivated student at Brooklyn Tech with strong communication skills and a passion for design. I've led my school's art club for two years.
answers.feedback: ✅ Perfect! Brief, professional, and highlights relevant strengths.

answers.text: I don't know, what do you want to know?
answers.feedback: This comes across as unprepared. Always have an answer ready!

answers.text: I'm the best candidate you'll meet today.
answers.feedback: Confidence is good, but this sounds arrogant without backing it up.

answers.text: I don't have any weaknesses.
answers.feedback: No one believes this! It makes you seem unaware or dishonest.

answers.text: I'm a perfectionist — I work too hard.
answers.feedback: This is a cliché. Interviewers have heard it a thousand times.

answers.text: I sometimes struggle with public speaking, but I've been practicing in my school debate club to improve.
answers.feedback: ✅ Honest, specific, and shows self-improvement. That's the formula!

answers.text: I hate mornings, so I might be late sometimes.
answers.feedback: Never hint at punctuality issues in an interview!

questions.question: You arrive 10 minutes early. The receptionist asks you to wait. You should:

answers.text: Pull out your phone and scroll social media.
answers.feedback: The receptionist may report this. Stay professional the whole time.

answers.text: Sit quietly, review your notes, and smile warmly at staff.
answers.feedback: ✅ You're always being evaluated — even in the waiting room!

answers.text: Ask the receptionist about the company culture.
answers.feedback: Receptionist isn't your interviewer. Don't put them in an awkward spot.

answers.text: Pace the lobby to calm your nerves.
answers.feedback: This looks anxious and unprofessional. Take slow breaths instead.

title: Write a Cover Letter That Works
subtitle: Say what your resume can't.
videoTitle: How to Write a Cover Letter — Step by Step
description: Craft a compelling cover letter that gets you noticed, even without experience. Stand out from the pile.
keyPoints: Open with energy — don't start with 'My name is...'
Explain why THIS company specifically excites you
Connect your skills to their actual job description
Keep it to 3 short paragraphs — less is more
End with a confident call-to-action

sections.title: The 3-Paragraph Formula
sections.content: Great cover letters have a simple structure. Paragraph 1: Hook them with your enthusiasm and mention the exact role. Paragraph 2: Show how your skills/experience match what they need (use their job listing's keywords!). Paragraph 3: Express excitement, mention your availability, and politely request an interview. That's it. No fluff.

sections.title: Personalize or Perish
sections.content: A generic cover letter is worse than no cover letter. Always name the company, reference the job title exactly, and show you know something about them. Did they win an award recently? Are they known for community work? A single specific detail shows you actually care. Hiring managers can smell copy-paste from a mile away.

title: Workplace Professionalism 101
subtitle: The unwritten rules of work.
videoTitle: Workplace Professionalism Tips for First-Time Workers
description: Learn what employers expect: punctuality, communication, dress code, and teamwork that makes you stand out.
keyPoints: Show up on time — being late is being disrespectful
Communicate clearly and respectfully with everyone
Ask questions instead of guessing — it saves everyone time
Your phone should be put away unless it's a break
Attitude matters as much as skill — bring positive energy

sections.title: The Punctuality Rule
sections.content: In the professional world, 'on time' means 5 minutes early. Being late signals that you don't value other people's time. If you're ever going to be late, call ahead as soon as you know — don't wait. And if you have a chronic punctuality issue, work backwards: what time do you need to leave home to arrive 10 minutes early? Set that alarm.

sections.title: Workplace Communication
sections.content: Email your boss with proper grammar — no emojis, abbreviations, or 'lol' in professional messages. When you don't understand something, ask for clarification instead of doing it wrong. Say 'thank you' and 'please.' Address older coworkers as Mr./Ms. unless they tell you otherwise. Small words make a huge impression.

sections.title: Dress Codes Decoded
sections.content: Business formal = suits and dress shoes. Business casual = clean slacks/khakis, collared shirts, simple dresses. Smart casual = neat jeans, blouses, clean sneakers. When in doubt, ask your manager before day one. Always dress slightly nicer than required — it shows you care and gets you noticed for promotions.

game.title: 🎮 Workplace Dilemmas — What Would You Do?
game.instructions: React to these real workplace situations. Choose the most professional response!

questions.question: Your manager asks you to stay 30 minutes late but you have plans. You say:

answers.text: Nah, I'm good, I have stuff.
answers.feedback: Too casual and unhelpful. This damages your professional reputation.

answers.text: I have a prior commitment today, but I'm happy to come in early tomorrow to help finish. Would that work?
answers.feedback: ✅ Respectful, solutions-focused, and shows initiative!

answers.text: Sure, no problem!' and then leave on time anyway.
answers.feedback: Never say yes and then do the opposite. Trust is everything.

answers.text: I'd rather not.
answers.feedback: Too blunt with no explanation or alternative offered.

questions.question: You made a mistake on a task your manager assigned. You should:

answers.text: Hope no one notices.
answers.feedback: Mistakes get discovered. Being proactive shows integrity.

answers.text: Blame a coworker to take the heat off.
answers.feedback: This is workplace sabotage. It destroys trust and your reputation.

answers.text: Tell your manager immediately, explain what happened, and suggest how you'll fix it.
answers.feedback: ✅ Owning mistakes quickly and coming with solutions shows real maturity.

answers.text: Quit before they find out.
answers.feedback: One mistake rarely costs you a job. How you handle it defines your character.

title: Understanding Your First Paycheck
subtitle: Why is my check smaller than I expected?
videoTitle: Understanding Your First Paycheck and Taxes
description: Decode taxes, deductions, net vs. gross pay, and what to do with your first earnings as a NYC young worker.
keyPoints: Gross pay = what you earn. Net pay = what you take home.
Federal, state, and city taxes are automatically deducted
FICA covers Social Security and Medicare — everyone pays this
Keep every pay stub — they're your financial proof
Start saving even a small amount from day one

sections.title: Gross vs. Net Pay
sections.content: You get hired at $17/hour. You work 40 hours. That's $680 gross pay — but you won't take home $680. After federal income tax (~10–12%), New York state tax (~4–6%), NYC city tax (~3%), and FICA (7.65% for Social Security + Medicare), you might take home around $550–$580. This is called your net pay. It's not your employer stealing from you — it's taxes that fund schools, roads, and social programs.

sections.title: Your W-4 Form Matters
sections.content: When you start a job, you fill out a W-4 form that tells your employer how much tax to withhold. If you're a dependent (your parents claim you), you'll likely be in the 0 allowances bracket. Each January, your employer gives you a W-2 form showing everything you earned and paid in taxes — you use this to file your tax return.

title: LinkedIn Profile Essentials
subtitle: Let recruiters find YOU.
videoTitle: How to Create a LinkedIn Profile for Students — Step by Step
description: Build a professional LinkedIn profile that attracts recruiters and opens doors before you even apply.
keyPoints: Use a professional headshot — no selfies, no party photos
Your headline should say who you are AND what you want
Write a first-person summary that sounds like YOU
Add every school project, club, and volunteer activity
Connect with teachers, mentors, and local professionals

sections.title: Why LinkedIn at Your Age?
sections.content: Over 90% of recruiters use LinkedIn to find candidates. Having a profile puts you in the game before you even start applying. Students with LinkedIn profiles get noticed for internships, scholarships, and mentorship programs. It's also where you can follow companies, see their culture, and learn about openings before they're posted elsewhere.

sections.title: Headline and About Section
sections.content: Your headline appears under your name and is the first thing anyone reads. Don't just say 'Student at Brooklyn Tech.' Say 'Aspiring Graphic Designer | Brooklyn Tech | Adobe Creative Suite | Looking for Summer Internship.' Pack in keywords! Your About section should be 3–5 sentences in first person: who you are, what you're studying/interested in, what you're looking for, and one personal detail that makes you memorable.

title: Networking for Beginners
subtitle: It's not what you know, it's who.
videoTitle: How to Network as a Student or Young Professional
description: How to make connections, ask for help, and grow your professional network in NYC even as a teen.
keyPoints: Networking is just making genuine human connections
Informational interviews are free and incredibly valuable
Give before you ask — offer help, share resources
Follow up within 24 hours after meeting someone
NYC has free networking events every week — attend them!

sections.title: What Networking Actually Means
sections.content: Forget the stereotype of handing out business cards at stuffy events. Modern networking is just building genuine relationships with people who share your interests or work in fields you care about. It can happen at a school event, through Instagram, via LinkedIn, at a community program, or through a mutual friend. The goal isn't to get something — it's to build real connections over time.

sections.title: The Informational Interview
sections.content: An informational interview is when you reach out to someone working in your dream field and ask them 15–20 minutes to learn about their career path. Not to ask for a job — just to learn. This is one of the most powerful career moves you can make. You get insider knowledge, they feel valued, and you now have a real contact in the industry who knows your name.

sections.title: Your Networking Message Template
sections.content: Keep outreach short and respectful. Try: 'Hi [Name], I'm [Your name], a high school junior interested in [their field]. I came across your work at [company] and was really inspired by [specific thing]. Would you have 15 minutes for a quick call? I'd love to hear about your career journey.' Simple, specific, and respectful of their time.

title: Google Workspace Basics
subtitle: The tools every job uses.
videoTitle: Google Workspace Tutorial for Beginners — Docs, Sheets, Slides
description: Master Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides — the suite of tools that nearly every modern workplace uses daily.
keyPoints: Google Docs is like Word — for writing and documents
Google Sheets is like Excel — for data and calculations
Google Slides is like PowerPoint — for presentations
Everything saves automatically to the cloud
Use @mentions and comments to collaborate in real-time

sections.title: Why Google Workspace?
sections.content: Over 6 million businesses use Google Workspace. Knowing how to use it puts you ahead of other applicants. Unlike Microsoft Office, everything is free with a Google account, saves automatically to Google Drive, and lets multiple people work on the same document at the same time. You can access it from any device, anywhere.

sections.title: Google Sheets Fundamentals
sections.content: Sheets might look scary but it's incredibly powerful. Key functions you need to know: SUM (adds numbers), AVERAGE, COUNT, and IF statements. Keyboard shortcuts save massive time: Ctrl+C to copy, Ctrl+V to paste, Ctrl+Z to undo, and Ctrl+Shift+= to insert a row. Even basic spreadsheet skills make you look like a tech wizard to older managers.

title: Budgeting on Your First Salary
subtitle: Make your money work for you.
description: Learn the 50/30/20 budgeting rule and start building wealth from your very first paycheck as a young worker.
keyPoints: The 50/30/20 rule: needs, wants, savings
Pay yourself first — savings come before fun money
An emergency fund of $500 changes your life
Avoid buy-now-pay-later schemes — they create debt
Even $20/week saved = $1,040 by end of the year

sections.title: The 50/30/20 Rule
sections.content: This simple framework works for any income. 50% goes to Needs — rent/transit/groceries/phone. 30% goes to Wants — eating out, entertainment, clothes, subscriptions. 20% goes to Savings — emergency fund, goals, future. As a teenager, your 'needs' might be much lower since you live at home, which means you can save a bigger percentage. This is the BEST financial advantage young workers have.

sections.title: Building Your Emergency Fund
sections.content: Life throws curveballs. Your phone breaks. You miss a week of work sick. Your MetroCard expires. Having $500–$1,000 in savings means these things are inconveniences, not crises. Start small: set a goal to save your first $100, then $250, then $500. Keep emergency money in a separate savings account so you're not tempted to spend it.

title: Behavioral Interview Questions
subtitle: Master the STAR method.
videoTitle: Answering Behavioral Interview Questions Using STAR
description: Answer 'Tell me about a time when...' questions with confidence using the proven STAR storytelling framework.
keyPoints: STAR = Situation, Task, Action, Result
Use real stories — specificity makes you memorable
Every story should show growth or problem-solving
Quantify results whenever possible ('increased by 30%')
Prepare at least 5 different stories before any interview

sections.title: Why Behavioral Questions?
sections.content: Employers believe past behavior predicts future performance. 'Tell me about a time you solved a conflict with a coworker' isn't just curiosity — it reveals how you actually handle stress. They want stories, not theories. 'I would handle it by...' is weak. 'When I was leading my school project and two teammates disagreed, I...' is powerful because it's real.

sections.title: Building Your Story Bank
sections.content: Before every interview, write out 5 'stories' using STAR. Pick situations from school, sports, volunteer work, family responsibilities — anything. Cover these themes: a time you solved a problem, showed leadership, failed and learned from it, went above and beyond, worked under pressure. Mix them, adapt them. You'll never be caught off guard.

title: Professional Email Writing
subtitle: Your words represent you.
videoTitle: How to Write Professional Emails — Full Guide
description: Write clear, professional emails that make you look polished, capable, and mature in the workplace.
keyPoints: Always use a clear subject line — no blank subjects
Open with a greeting: 'Hi [Name],' or 'Dear [Title] [Name],'
State your purpose in the first sentence
Keep it short — if it's longer than 5 sentences, restructure
End with 'Best regards' or 'Thank you' + your full name

sections.title: The Anatomy of a Professional Email
sections.content: Every professional email has the same structure: (1) Subject line — clear and specific. (2) Greeting — 'Hi Sarah,' or 'Dear Mr. Johnson,' not 'Hey' or nothing. (3) Opening line — get to the point. (4) Body — keep it concise and focused. (5) Call to action — what do you need them to do? (6) Sign-off — 'Best regards,' 'Thank you,' or 'Sincerely.' Your name and contact info.

sections.title: Common Email Mistakes That Kill Credibility
sections.content: Never reply-all when you meant to reply. Never send an email in all caps (it reads as shouting). Don't use slang like 'u,' 'lmk,' 'omg.' Re-read every email before sending — read it out loud to catch errors. Don't put anything in an email you wouldn't say to their face. Emails are permanent records.

title: Cybersecurity at Work
subtitle: Protect yourself and your employer.
videoTitle: Cybersecurity Basics for Everyone — Stay Safe Online
description: Protect yourself and your employer with essential cybersecurity practices every worker needs to know today.
keyPoints: Use strong, unique passwords for every account
Enable two-factor authentication on everything
Never click suspicious links — even from coworkers
Don't share login credentials with anyone
Use company Wi-Fi only for work, not personal banking

sections.title: Why This Matters at Work
sections.content: Data breaches cost companies millions, but they often start with one employee clicking the wrong link. As an entry-level worker, you're often the target of phishing emails because attackers know you're new and less trained. One click can compromise the entire company's data — and that could cost you your job and create serious legal issues.

sections.title: Password Security 101
sections.content: A strong password has 12+ characters, uses uppercase, lowercase, numbers, and symbols, and isn't a word you'd find in a dictionary. Never reuse passwords. Use a password manager like LastPass or Bitwarden to remember them. Never share your password — not even with IT staff (they don't need it). Enable two-factor authentication (2FA) wherever possible.
